title: Kanungum / Conungum
summary: Kanungum, also written Conungum or Conungam, names a pond widening the Peconic River at Calverton in Tooker’s account of Southampton’s northwestern boundary.
introduction_content: A river and a boundary meet in the name Kanungum. Tooker identifies it as a pond through which the Peconic River passes at Calverton, also recorded as Conungum and Conungam. Tooker (1911), pp. 76–77.
history_content: Tooker cites a reference to Kanungum Pond in Southampton’s proprietors’ records and reproduces Nathaniel Prime’s description of the town boundary passing through the pond before turning south toward Seatuck Creek. This connects the name with the recording of town limits as well as a water feature. Tooker (1911), pp. 76–77.
translation_content:
Tooker interprets Kanungum as a boundary-related name. His discussion of a “boundary village” concerns a comparison in Massachusetts, rather than evidence for a village at Calverton. His linguistic interpretation is historical and remains open to community scholarship. Tooker (1911), pp. 76–77.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names represent a convergence of Indigenous language, history, culture, and environmental knowledge.”

— Xatśūll First Nation, Cumulative Effects Knowledge and Land Use Evaluation Study (2024), Place-name discussion, PDF page 92

Kanungum connects Indigenous place naming with the river landscape and the boundaries later written into town records. Reading the waterway alongside those records helps explain how an older name continued to shape the geography of Calverton.
land_loss_content: Kanungum connects Indigenous place naming with the river landscape and the boundaries later written into town records. Reading the waterway alongside those records helps explain how an older name continued to shape the geography of Calverton.
whereintheworld_content: Kanungum belongs to the Peconic River landscape at Calverton. Tooker describes a pond formed by a widening of the river at Southampton’s northwestern boundary. Its exact correspondence with today’s river and pond edges remains uncertain; the map marks the wider Calverton locality. Tooker (1911), pp. 76–77.
